previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A man with end-stage renal disease, type 2 diabetes, Chagas-related cardiomyopathy, and recent pleurodesis was readmitted for persistent fever, productive cough with yellow sputum, and a mechanical fall. He had been discharged recently after a viral syndrome and pleural effusion. On admission, he was febrile with elevated white count and imaging showing a loculated right pleural effusion and atelectasis. He was treated empirically for healthcare-associated pneumonia with vancomycin and Zosyn. Blood and sputum cultures remained negative. His fever and cough resolved, and the right pleural catheter was removed. He completed five days of IV antibiotics in hospital and was discharged on a 10-day course with oral levofloxacin and dialysis-administered vancomycin. His hip X-ray showed no fracture, and pain was managed with acetaminophen and oxycodone. Lisinopril was temporarily reduced and then increased back toward home dose. He was discharged home with services and follow-up plans.

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ is a ___ year old man with a history of ESRD 
previously on HD who started PD 2 weeks prior to admission and 
presented with 24 hours of abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting 
secondary to peritonitis.  

# Peritonitis: Paitent with proven PD peritonitis with WBC is 
greater than 100. Empiric coverage was started with a third 
generation cephalosporin and vancomycin which after the first IV 
doses of Vancomycin and Ceftriaxone were transitioned to 
intraperitoneal ceftazidime and vancomycin. By 12 hours after 
initiation of antibiotics, Mr. ___ was feeling better and his 
abdominal pain had resolved. Vancomycin was held after the 
second dose as his daily trough was too high (> 20). He will 
remain on antibiotics for a total of ___ weeks, unfortunately no 
cultures were grown and he will remain on empiric therapy with 
vancomycin and ceftazidime. 
   Concern was given to the fact that Mr. ___ had just 
started peritoneal dialysis and had already suffered 
peritonitis. His family was re-educated regarding hygiene 
associated with peritoneal dialysis. His wife expressed concern 
that she felt overwhelmed with peritoneal dialysis, and PD may 
not be the best dialysis modality going forward.
 
# DIABETES TYPE I: Lantus was continued. 

# END STAGE RENAL DISEASE: Nephrocaps, sensipar, and renvela 
were continued.
 
# CAD:  Carvedilol, pravastatin, lisinopril, and aspirin were 
continued.
 
# HYPERLIPIDEMIA : Pravastatin was continued.

Transitional Issues:
- Mr. ___ wife expressed concern that she felt overwhelmed 
with peritoneal dialysis. PD may not be the best dialysis 
modality going forward given his episode of peritonitis so soon 
after initiation.

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  ___ male with diffuse abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting
after peritoneal dialysis; question perforation.

COMPARISON:  ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Helical CT images were acquired of the abdomen and pelvis
following the administration of oral contrast only, and reformatted into
coronal and sagittal planes.

FINDINGS:

LUNG BASES:  Round atelectasis is noted in the right lower lobe posteriorly. 
There is adjacent pleural calcification.  There is also minimal atelectasis of
the left base.  The coronary arteries are diffusely calcified.

ABDOMEN:  Evaluation of solid abdominal viscera is limited by lack of
intravenous contrast.  Within these limitations, the liver is normal in
appearance without intrahepatic biliary ductal dilatation.  The spleen is
normal.  Fatty pancreas is normal in appearance.  The adrenals are normal
bilaterally.  Cholecystectomy clips are seen in the gallbladder fossa.  The
kidneys are shrunken bilaterally.

The stomach is filled with positive contrast and appears normal.  Loops of
small bowel are normal in caliber.  The small bowel mesentery appears normal. 
There is no intraperitoneal free fluid or free air.  Note is made of median
sternotomy wires anteriorly in the chest.

The bladder is collapsed.  A peritoneal dialysis catheter is noted in pelvis. 
The prostate is unremarkable.  The colon is normal appearing.  The appendix is
normal.

There is no osseous abnormality.

A central venous catheter tip projects over the right atrium.

IMPRESSION:
1.  No evidence of perforation or acute abdominal abnormality.

2.  Round atelectasis in the right lower lobe.

3.  Coronary arterial calcification.
